Operator: Good morning, and welcome to the Apex Insurance Group Second Quarter 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. As a reminder, this conference is being recorded. [Standard operator instructions for Q&A participation.]

I would now like to turn the conference over to Sarah Thompson, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Thompson: Thank you, Operator, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to Apex Insurance Group's Q2 2024 earnings call. Joining me on the call today are John Reynolds, Chief Executive Officer; Michael Chen, Chief Financial Officer; Lisa Patel, Chief Underwriting Officer; David Wong, Chief Investment Officer; and Emily Rivera, Chief Operating Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that some of the statements we are making today may be considered forward-looking. These statements are subject to certain risks and uncertainties that could cause our actual results to differ materially from those projected. We encourage you to review our SEC filings for a more detailed discussion of these risks and uncertainties.

I will now turn the call over to John Reynolds.

John Reynolds: Thank you, Sarah, and good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us today. I'm pleased to report on Apex Insurance Group's performance for the second quarter of 2024. We delivered strong results, driven by robust gross written premium growth across key lines, improved underwriting discipline amid loss ratio pressures, effective management of catastrophe losses, solid reinsurance recoveries, and enhanced investment yields from a diversified portfolio. We are particularly excited about the initial success of our StormShield Elite product and its rapid adoption in high-risk regions, blending traditional property coverage with parametric overlays for faster claims resolution.

Michael, our CFO, will now provide a more detailed review of our financial performance.

Michael Chen: Thank you, John. Good morning, everyone. As John mentioned, we had a solid quarter. Our net income was $450 million, or $1.85 per share. Key drivers of our financial performance included double-digit premium expansion, favorable prior-year development, disciplined expense management, and resilient investment returns. Our combined ratio was 95.2%. Investment income for the quarter was $320 million, reflecting strong performance in our fixed income and alternatives segments. We continue to maintain a strong capital position, with $12.5 billion in surplus.

Let me dive deeper into our results, starting with our loss ratio performance, a core metric for our property and casualty underwriting discipline here at Apex Insurance Group. For the second quarter, our consolidated calendar-year loss ratio came in at 62.5%, a 230 basis point deterioration from 60.2% in Q2 of last year, but right in line with our guided range of 61-64% for the full year 2024. This reflects a dynamic environment, but importantly, our accident-year loss ratio improved to 61.8%, benefiting from 150 basis points of favorable prior-year development, primarily in our personal auto and workers' compensation books.

Breaking this down by key drivers—claims frequency and severity, with some regional insights and the technical actions we're taking to mitigate pressures—our personal lines, which represent 55% of earned premiums, saw a loss ratio of 65.2%, up from 62.8% prior year, driven largely by auto. Commercial lines held steady at a superior 58.1%, thanks to our focus on middle-market risks with strong loss control services.

Claims frequency remains foundational, and we've seen a modest uptick across the board. In personal auto—our largest segment at $2.8 billion in Q2 earned premiums—reported claims frequency rose 2.1% year-over-year, aligning with industry data from ISO and Verisk Analytics showing a similar 1.8-2.5% increase. This is largely attributable to normalizing driving patterns post-COVID; vehicle miles traveled is now 5% above 2019 levels per FHWA data, coupled with persistent distracted driving—our telematics data pegs smartphone usage at 12% of trips. We've also noted a 3% frequency bump in severe weather-related homeowners claims, tied to an active Atlantic hurricane season start, with three named storms already making landfall.

On a brighter note, our commercial auto frequency was flat at 1.12 claims per 100 vehicles, benefiting from our fleet telematics partnerships with Verizon Connect and Geotab, which have reduced at-fault incidents by 8% in participating accounts. Workers' comp frequency declined 1.5% to 0.92 claims per $100 payroll, aided by return-to-work programs and our integration of AI-driven risk assessments from vendors like EagleView for workplace safety scoring.

Severity is the real headwind, inflating faster than our pricing—up 5.6% year-over-year on a trend-adjusted basis. In personal auto, average claim costs hit $4,750, a 6.2% increase, fueled by parts inflation (up 12% per CCC Intelligent Solutions data) and labor rates at body shops averaging $52 per hour, up from $48. Supply chain disruptions for OEM parts, like those lingering from the chip shortage, are exacerbating this, with repair cycle times stretching to 28 days from 22. Medical severity in auto PIP and no-fault states like Michigan and Florida rose 7.1%, mirroring national healthcare CPI at 4.5% but amplified by rising chiropractic and PT costs.

Homeowners severity jumped 8.4% to $18,200 per claim, driven by material costs—lumber up 9%, rebar 11%—and labor shortages in catastrophe-prone regions. A prime example: California wildfires, where our $150 million net loss from the Park Fire reflected higher rebuild costs amid zoning restrictions and skilled labor premiums. Commercial lines severity moderated to +4.2%, with general liability holding the line through better subrogation rates—our recovery rate hit 92% via partnerships with Crawford & Company.

Regionally, in the U.S., which is 70% of our book, Midwest and Northeast personal auto severity is +6.8% due to rust repair and dense urban claims, while Southeast homeowners frequency is up 4% from convective storms. Europe, 15% of premiums, benefited from milder weather, with UK motor severity at +3.9% versus our +5.6% global, thanks to Motor Insurance Database pricing discipline. In Asia-Pacific, Australia severity spiked 7.2% from floods, but our reinsurance tower—100% quota share above $50 million—capped net impact at $20 million.

We're not standing still. On the tech front, we've rolled out GenAI claims triage across 85% of our auto adjusters, reducing cycle time by 22% and initial reserve accuracy to within 5% of ultimate, per our internal actual versus ultimate reserve metrics. This mirrors Progressive's Snapshot model but scaled with our 15 million policy telematics dataset, which flags high-risk drivers pre-loss—dropping frequency 4% in opted-in segments.

Underwriting-wise, we've taken 9.2% rate across personal auto since Q4 2023, with another 6-8% renewals planned for H2, targeting a 68% permitted rate need per our actuarial models. We've also optimized our book: non-renewing 12% of underperforming California homeowners (high wildfire exposure) and shifting to preferred risk tiers, boosting our auto credit score segmentation—now 65% A/B tiers versus 58% last year. Reinsurance renewal in January was disciplined: our probable maximum loss for a 1-in-100 year cat event is $450 million net, down 5% via higher attachments and sidecars from Swiss Re and RenaissanceRe.

Strategically, this positions us for margin expansion. Our combined ratio target remains 95% for 2025, with loss ratio improvement to 60-62% via frequency stabilization (expecting VMT growth to slow to 1%) and severity moderation as supply chains normalize—projecting +4% trend versus +5.6% this year. We're leaning into usage-based insurance, with UBI penetration at 28% and 15% lower loss ratios than traditional policies. Compared to peers like Allstate (Q2 loss ratio 68.4%) and Travelers (64.2%), our discipline shines, and we're gaining share in commercial E&S lines, up 14% YoY.

Next, a critical metric: total catastrophe losses impact, which we report both in absolute USD terms and as a percentage of gross written premium. For Q2, our total catastrophe losses came in at $1.45 billion pre-tax, representing 9.2% of GWP. To contextualize, our Q2 GWP grew 7% year-over-year to $15.8 billion, driven by mid-single-digit rate increases in US commercial property and strong renewal retention in our international specialty lines. This cat load marks a sequential increase from Q1's $850 million or 5.8% of GWP, but it's down 12% from Q2 2023's elevated $1.65 billion—or 11.5% of GWP—when we absorbed outsized hits from Hurricane Ian and European windstorms like Eunice.

Breaking it down by event and region, the US accounted for 65% of our Q2 cat losses, or $940 million, primarily from Hurricanes Idalia and Lee battering our Florida and Gulf Coast homeowners portfolios. Our industry loss estimates, per RMS modeling, pegged Idalia at a $12 billion industry aggregate total event, and we captured about 7.8% market share there—right in line with our 8% Florida homeowners penetration. Florida remains a hotspot, with our state-specific PML now at 15% of surplus post our 2023 quota share reinsurance renewal, up from 12% last year due to escalating rebuild costs and secondary perils like storm surge.

Internationally, Asia-Pacific contributed 22%, or $320 million, led by Typhoon Saola in the Philippines and Japan, impacting our facultative reinsurance placements with partners like Munich Re. We saw favorable development here from our parametric trigger products, which accelerated $150 million in payouts via satellite-verified wind speeds exceeding 120 km/h—a game-changer for basis risk mitigation. Europe and Australia rounded out the rest at 8% and 5%, respectively, with wildfires in New South Wales driving $70 million against our Australian composite book.

On the P&L impact: These cats widened our all-accident-year combined ratio to 102.4% in Q2, versus an ex-cat ratio of 92.1%—a solid improvement from 94.5% ex-cat in Q1, reflecting our earned rate discipline and expense ratio leverage to 28.9%. Net income absorbed a $950 million hit after reinsurance recoveries, which covered 35% via our multi-year tower: a $500 million excess-of-loss layer attaching at $750 million, plus sidecar contributions from our $1.2 billion New Zealand cat bond issuance earlier this year. This kept our loss ratio at 68.2% all-cat, compared to peers like Travelers at 72% or Chubb at 70% on similar exposure.

Trend-wise, we're projecting full-year 2024 total cat losses at $4.2 billion, or 7.8% of full-year GWP, up from 6.2% in 2023 but below our 1-in-50 year stress test of 10.5%. Climate attribution modeling from AIR Worldwide shows a 25% uptick in frequency for US convective storms and APAC typhoons over the past decade, aligning with IPCC AR6 projections. We've responded aggressively: implemented 12-15% cat-load pricing hikes in Florida and California renewals, with dynamic cat pricing via AI-driven APIs integrating Verisk Touchstone models. This has de-risked our book by 18% in attritional loss ratio terms.

We've expanded our third-party capital platform to $2.5 billion, including two new insurance-linked securities cat bonds priced at 450 bps spread, collateralizing our US hurricane excess layer. We're also piloting collateralized reinsurance with Lombard Street on European flood perils. Reduced gross NAT CAT exposure by 10% YoY through non-renewals in high-hazard ZIP codes, boosting geographic diversification—now 45% US, 25% Europe/MENA, 20% APAC, and 10% LatAm/RoW. We've doubled down on cyber-physical hybrid products like StormShield Elite with Allianz.

Rolled out our proprietary CatRisk Engine 2.0, leveraging machine learning on 20 years of EM-DAT data and NOAA satellite feeds, which improved our loss reserve accuracy by 22% in Q2—evidenced by $180 million favorable prior-year development.

Strategically, cats underscore our fortress balance sheet ethos: leverage at 2.1x, risk-based capital at 220% of RBC, and $8.5 billion in liquid assets for peak season deployability. We're not chasing volume in cat-heavy markets; instead, we're premium accretive, targeting 95% ex-cat COR long-term. As peers like Progressive pull back from California fire exposure, we're gaining share in derisked segments like US excess & surplus, up 14% YoY.

Turning to top-line results, Gross Written Premiums, or GWP, grew 12.4% year-over-year to $8.7 billion in the second quarter. This marks our strongest quarterly GWP growth since Q4 2021, driven by disciplined pricing, robust new business flows, and targeted expansion in high-margin lines. Excluding the impact of foreign exchange headwinds in Europe—down 2% on a constant currency basis—organic GWP growth accelerated to 13.8%, underscoring our rate adequacy and retention momentum.

By line of business, Personal Lines, 42% of our total GWP, grew 14.2% YoY to $3.7 billion. Personal Auto was the standout, up 16.5% to $2.4 billion, fueled by a 9% average rate increase—our third consecutive quarter of double-digit hikes—amid persistent inflation in repair costs, parts shortages, and bodily injury claims severity up 7% linked to medical trends. New business acquisition surged 22%, thanks to our telematics-enabled DriveSafe UBI program, now active with 1.2 million policies and delivering a 15% better loss ratio than our book average. Homeowners & Dwellings grew a solid 10.8% to $1.3 billion, benefiting from 7% rate uplift and 12% policy count growth in catastrophe-exposed regions like Florida and California, where we've leaned into risk-adequate pricing post-Hurricane Ian. Retention held steady at 88%, above industry peers like Progressive and State Farm.

Commercial Lines, 35% of GWP, up 9.7% YoY to $3.0 billion. This line faced some softening in middle-market competition, but we offset it with premium per risk growth of 8%. Workers' Compensation expanded 11.2% to $1.1 billion, driven by payroll inflation adjustments and our AI-powered underwriting platform, which improved quote turnaround by 40% and selective risk appetite in high-hazard industries like construction. General Liability and Umbrella lines grew 8.5%, though we ceded some low-margin fleet auto renewals to focus on our EnterpriseGuard bundled packages, capturing 5% market share in the SMB segment per AM Best data. Challenges persist from softening rates in excess & surplus—down 2% industry-wide—but our 92% retention and 6% new business growth kept us ahead of Travelers and The Hartford.

Specialty and Global Markets, our highest-margin segment at 15% of GWP, delivered explosive 21.3% growth to $1.3 billion, outpacing Chubb and AXA XL. Marine and Energy lines surged 25% on the back of geopolitical volatility boosting hull and cargo demand, with our parametric trigger products—launched last year—now covering $2 billion in notional exposure and paying out 30% faster than traditional claims. Cyber insurance grew 18%, reflecting enterprise demand amid rising ransomware incidents; we've embedded third-party cyber risk scoring from partners like Cyence, achieving a 65% attachment rate on new quotes. Regionally, APAC Specialty doubled to $450 million, led by expansion in Singapore and Australia via our JV with Ping An, tapping into infrastructure boom risks.

Life & Health, 8% of GWP, grew a more modest 6.2% to $700 million, in line with sector dynamics. Group Life and Disability benefited from 5% rate re-pricing and enrollment growth in US employer-sponsored plans, while our term life book expanded 7% through digital distribution partnerships with banks like Wells Fargo. Health reinsurance—our niche play—saw 9% uplift from longevity and morbidity trends, though US ACA exchange volatility capped upside.

These results reflect our Precision Pricing 2.0 initiative, leveraging catastrophe modeling from RMS and machine learning for granular rate segmentation, which contributed 400 basis points to overall growth. Regionally, US GWP rose 15% (55% of total), Europe 8% despite regulatory rate caps under Solvency II, and Emerging Markets 22% as we scale in India and Brazil with micro-insurance products. Looking ahead, we expect full-year GWP growth of 11-13%, with tailwinds from continued hardening in P&C markets—per Verisk analytics, auto rates up 12% industry-wide—and our $500 million tech investment in cloud-based policy admin systems to boost cross-sell ratios by 200 bps.

Reinsurance recoveries are a critical component of our P&C underwriting performance that helped drive our strong quarter. In Q2 2024, we received $285 million in reinsurance recoveries, up 22% from the $233 million collected in Q2 2023 and 18% sequentially from Q1 this year. Year-to-date through June 30, we've pulled in $512 million, putting us on track for a full-year receipt pace of around $1.1 billion. These inflows directly bolstered our combined ratio to 92.8% ex-cat, well below our 95% target, and contributed 15 basis points to our return on equity expansion to 13.2%.

These recoveries stem primarily from our excess-of-loss and quota share treaties, with a weighted average recovery rate of 68% on paid gross losses this quarter—up from 64% last year. This improvement reflects both favorable prior-year development and timely cedings under our multi-year programs. Notably, we saw $142 million in recoveries tied to 2023 catastrophe events, including Hurricane Idalia and the Maui wildfires, where our attachment points held firm at $150 million per risk layer for U.S. property cat.

Shifting to expected recoveries, our actuaries project an additional $420 million over the next 12 months, with $210 million anticipated in H2 2024 alone. This pipeline is conservatively estimated using our internal ultimate loss models, benchmarked against RMS v18.1 and AIR Worldwide catastrophe platforms, and assumes a 5% discount rate for timing adjustments. Breaking it down by vintage: $180 million from 2023 events (now at 92% paid-to-ultimate), $150 million from 2022 California wildfires (with ongoing subrogation recoveries boosting cessions), and $90 million from 2024 secondary perils like the European winter storms and Australian floods.

Regionally, in North America, 55% of our gross losses, U.S. recoveries totaled $157 million received YTD, driven by our facultative placements with Swiss Re and Munich Re on Florida property risks. We've seen excellent performance here, with recovery rates hitting 72% versus our 65% modeled expectation, thanks to tight wording on event aggregation and index triggers. However, we're monitoring Hurricane Beryl's early impacts, where we expect $45 million in net recoveries from our $2.5 billion tower, layered above a $200 million retention.

Europe contributed $98 million in receipts, up 30% YoY, largely from reinstatement premiums on our proportional D&O treaties with RenaissanceRe following the U.K. liability spike. Recovery rates here are at 65%, tempered by some disputes on cyber sub-limits, but our collateral requirements—100% trusts for non-rated reinsurers—have minimized leakage. In Asia-Pacific, a bright spot with $112 million expected from typhoon Gaemi and secondary perils; our partnership with Berkshire Hathaway on surplus share for Japanese earthquake exposure has yielded a 75% recovery rate, far exceeding peers amid Japan's tightening retro market.

Over the past five years, our cumulative recovery rate has climbed from 58% to 70%, correlating with our shift toward higher-quality panels—now 85% rated A or better by AM Best. Ceded premiums as a percentage of gross have stabilized at 28%, down from 32% in 2021, reflecting proactive risk selection via our proprietary AegisCat modeling engine, which integrates climate analytics from Climate X and satellite data from Planet Labs.

Post-January 1 renewals, our property cat program features 120% reinstatements on key layers, with a blended rate-on-line increase of just 2.5% despite $110 billion industry cat losses last year. We've diversified away from over-reliance on Bermuda names—now only 15% of capacity versus 25% in 2022—favoring U.S. and European sidecars like our $300 million quota share with Stone Ridge for U.S. Midwest tornadoes. On the alternative risk transfer front, our $150 million cat bond issuance via Securis—upside protected with parametric triggers—has unlocked $25 million in early recoveries from 2024 U.S. convective storms, at a cost of just 4% coupons.

We expect reinsurance recoveries to remain a tailwind, supporting our 10-12% organic growth guidance. Rising secondary perils (up 15% frequency per Verisk analytics) and La Niña's potential for Atlantic activity could pressure H2 net ratios by 100-200 points if we hit a 1-in-50 year event. Our response? Doubling down on portfolio steering—capping gross exposure at $1.2 billion per zone—and piloting index-linked covers for flood, which could shave 5 points off our attritional loss ratio by year-end.

Lisa, over to you for underwriting updates.

Lisa Patel: Thank you, Michael. I'd like to provide an update on our underwriting performance. We've seen continued strong performance in our commercial lines. We are actively managing our exposure to catastrophe risks and have implemented several initiatives to improve our risk selection, including AI-powered underwriting platforms, telematics integrations, and non-renewals in high-hazard areas, as Michael outlined. Our focus on middle-market and specialty risks, combined with rate adequacy and tech-driven triage, positions us well for sustained profitability.

David, please take us through investments.

David Wong: Thank you. From an investment perspective, we have continued to focus on diversifying our portfolio and managing risk in the current market environment. We are seeing positive returns from our investments in fixed income, equities, and alternatives.

Our general account invested assets stand at $285 billion as of June 30, up 4% year-over-year, reflecting strong premium growth in our life, annuity, and P&C segments, partially offset by strategic portfolio repositioning amid the higher-for-longer rate environment. Our portfolio is meticulously managed through our Asset Liability Management framework, targeting a duration match of 8.2 years—closely aligned with our $210 billion in policyholder liabilities, primarily long-duration annuities and whole life products. We adhere to NAIC Risk-Based Capital guidelines, maintaining a robust C-1 RBC ratio of 520%, well above our 400% target. Credit quality remains investment-grade dominant at 92% (A-rated or better per Moody's), with an average book yield of 4.8% and a marked-to-market portfolio yield of 5.2%, benefiting from the Fed's 525 bps fed funds rate and the Treasury curve steepening.

Fixed income: 72% of portfolio ($205 billion). This allocation ticked down 2 percentage points YoY from 74%, as we trimmed duration in light of inverted yield curves earlier in the cycle. Corporate bonds dominate at 45% of the sleeve ($92 billion), with a focus on financials (25% overweight vs. Bloomberg US Corporate Index) and utilities (15%), yielding 5.6% on a yield-to-worst basis. Investment-grade municipals comprise 18% ($37 billion), offering tax-efficient income for our domestic P&C book, with durations averaging 7.5 years. Structured credits, including agency MBS and ABS, make up 22% ($45 billion), where we've leaned into non-agency RMBS backed by prime jumbo loans—now 8% of the portfolio—targeting spreads of 150 bps over swaps. Government securities, including US Treasuries and TIPS, sit at 15% ($31 billion) for liquidity management, with our short-end ladder providing 12-month liquidity coverage at 1.5x stressed outflows per our internal ALM stress tests. Regionally, 65% is US-centric, with 20% in Eurozone sovereigns (e.g., German Bunds) and 10% in investment-grade Asian credits like Singaporean and Australian corporates, hedging our growing APAC annuity sales. Yields here compressed 25 bps QoQ on ECB rate cuts, prompting us to deploy $2.5 billion into UK gilts at 4.9% YTMs.

Equities: 13% of portfolio ($37 billion). We're at the high end of our 10-15% strategic band, up from 11% YoY, as equity risk premiums normalized post-2022 drawdowns. Public equities total $30 billion (81% of sleeve), benchmarked to the MSCI World Index, with a beta of 0.85 for downside protection. Sector allocation favors defensives: healthcare (28%, e.g., UnitedHealth, Johnson & Johnson), consumer staples (22%), and tech (18%, quality names like Microsoft and Visa). We've reduced cyclicals to 12% amid softening PMIs. Regionally, 55% US, 25% Europe (e.g., Nestlé, Roche), and 15% Japan (TOPIX value tilt), where yen repatriation flows boosted returns. Private equities via evergreen funds add $7 billion (19%), targeting 12-15% IRRs through secondaries in buyout funds from KKR and Blackstone. Q2 total return was 6.2%, driven by AI tailwinds, outpacing the S&P 500's 5.8%.

Alternatives: 15% of portfolio ($43 billion), up 3 points YoY to 15%, within our 12-18% band, as we navigate compressed IG spreads. This sleeve delivered a 9.1% annualized return over the past 12 months, net of 1.2% fees. Real assets at 40% ($17 billion), including core real estate ($10 billion, 5.8% cap rates in multifamily and industrial via PGIM and LaSalle partnerships) and infrastructure ($7 billion, 7.2% yields from renewables like solar farms, aligning with our net-zero by 2050 commitment). Hedge funds and private credit round out at 35% ($15 billion, targeting 8-10% net IRRs) and private equity at 25% ($11 billion), with $3 billion in dry powder for 2024 vintages focused on insurance-tech and mid-market LBOs. We've initiated a $1 billion allocation to catastrophe bonds via our ILS platform, yielding 9.5% with low correlation to public markets—perfect for diversifying P&C tail risks.

Portfolio-wide, we're seeing book yield expansion to 4.9% from 4.2% YoY, thanks to $15 billion in reinvestments at current levels, but NAV pressure from prior rate volatility shaved 1.2% off Q2 returns. Volatility remains contained, with VaR at 4.1% (99% confidence, 10-day horizon). We've rolled out BlackRock's Aladdin platform enhancements for real-time ESG screening and scenario analysis, integrating climate risk models compliant with NAIC's evolving climate RBC charges. This supports our $50 billion sustainable fixed income mandate, 20% of total FI. In this disinflationary environment with 10Y Treasuries at 4.3%, we're de-risking via $5 billion in LDI overlays to lock in spreads, while hunting yield in private credit amid bank retrenchment—aiming for 100 bps pickup over publics. Regionally, US dominance persists for liquidity, but we're scaling EM exposure to 5% tied to our 15% APAC premium growth. We expect alternatives to grow to 17% by year-end, equities stable, and FI yields holding mid-5s, supporting 12-14% ROE expansion.

Specifically on investment income yield, it came in at 4.6% for the quarter on a trailing twelve-month basis—up 70 basis points year-over-year and marking our strongest quarterly reading since Q4 2021. This represents an annualized investment income of $1.2 billion on average invested assets of $26.1 billion, a meaningful contributor to our overall ROE of 12.8% this quarter. Our book yield stood at 4.2% at quarter-end, while the earned yield was 4.6%. This outperformance versus our long-term target range of 4.0% to 4.5% reflects favorable reinvestment opportunities and proactive optimization. Year-to-date, we've realized $850 million in net investment income, a 15% increase, driven by the Fed's hiking cycle, pushing the 10-year Treasury yield to 4.8% and BBB corporate spread to 145 basis points.

Fixed maturities remain core at 72%, with AA- average credit quality and 5.8-year duration. Investment-grade corporates 38% (up from 32%), yielding 5.1%; ABS 12% at 5.5%; municipals 8% with tax-equivalent yields over 6%. Equities steady at 15%, dividend yield 2.8% from blue-chips, plus REITs at 4.2%. Alternatives 11%, including core-plus real estate and ILS/cat bonds at 7-9%. U.S.-centric (85%), reinvestment rates 5.3% vs. maturities 3.9%. ALM stress tests show resilience; AI credit surveillance via Aladdin scans 50,000+ issuers. 45% new FI ESG-compliant. Q4 yields 5.0-5.4%; maintaining $4.2 billion cash with swaptions. This turns our $28 billion float into high-single-digit ROA, ahead of peers.

Operator, we are now ready to open the line for questions.

Operator: Thank you. [Operator instructions.] Our first question comes from Alex Rivera with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

Alex Rivera: Good morning. Can you provide more color on GWP growth by line of business?

Michael Chen: Good morning, Alex. As I detailed, GWP grew 12.4% to $8.7 billion, with personal lines up 14.2% led by 16.5% in auto from 9% rates and UBI surge; homeowners 10.8%; commercial 9.7% with workers' comp at 11.2%; specialty 21.3% on marine/energy/cyber; life/health 6.2%. Organic 13.8% ex-FX, full-year 11-13% outlook.

Operator: Our next question comes from Jamie Lee with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

Jamie Lee: Good morning. Could you discuss the impact of inflation on your business?

John Reynolds: Good morning, Jamie. Inflation, particularly in claims severity—up 5.6% overall, auto parts 12%, labor $52/hour—has been a headwind, but we've countered with 9.2% auto rates, tech triage cutting cycle times 22%, and portfolio optimization. Expects moderation to +4% trend.

Operator: Our next question comes from Chris Patel with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Chris Patel: What is the expected impact of Solvency II changes on your underwriting strategy?

Lisa Patel: Good morning, Chris. Solvency II rate caps in Europe have tempered growth to 8%, but our Precision Pricing 2.0 and RMS modeling ensure adequacy. We're diversifying geographically—45% US now—and focusing on high-margin specialty, maintaining 95% ex-cat COR target.

Operator: Our next question from Taylor Kim with Barclays.

Taylor Kim: On cat losses and reinsurance—any updates on expected recoveries?

Michael Chen: Taylor, Q2 cats $1.45B or 9.2% GWP; $285M received, $420M expected next 12 months. 68% recovery rate, strong from US/Europe/APAC panels. Renewals at +2.5% RoL, diversified sidecars/cat bonds protecting H2.

Operator: Next from Rachel Gomez with Citi.

Rachel Gomez: Thoughts on investment yield sustainability?

David Wong: Rachel, 4.6% TTM yield solid, book 4.2%/earned 4.6%; reinvestments at 5.3%, FI mid-5s hold. Alternatives 9.1% return, ILS 9.5%; ALM resilient to cuts/recession.

Operator: That concludes our Q&A. Thank you.

John Reynolds: Thank you for your questions and your interest in Apex Insurance Group. In closing, we are confident in our ability to continue delivering strong results and creating value for our shareholders. Thank you for joining us today.

Operator: This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for your participation. You may now disconnect.
